summary_student.text: Small gas flames of fuels such as methane, ethylene and propane were burned inside a glovebox on the International Space Station, with a gentle stream of air flowing around them. The team looked for the point where each flame starts to give off soot, which is what makes smoke. Knowing how and when flames make soot without gravity helps design safer spacecraft.

summary_professional.text: Laminar jet diffusion flames of methane, ethylene, propane, propylene and propylene mixtures were burned in co-flowing air in a flow duct inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox on the ISS. Burner diameters were 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm and 1.6 mm, and co-flow velocities ranged from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s; fuel flow rate was varied to find the laminar smoke point. Still and video cameras recorded luminous flame length and height, along with radiative heat losses and co-flow air velocity distributions, for 526 flames in total.

pillar.reason: The investigation characterizes soot formation and smoke points of non-buoyant flames, which the record says will help design safer spacecraft environments and refine models predicting flame behavior; it does not test detectors or extinguishment.

environments.reason: The flames were burned aboard the International Space Station, in the Microgravity Science Glovebox.
The tests describe flames without gravity-driven flow (microgravity), the condition of a vehicle in transit; the record itself does not name transit vehicles.
